newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-ADJUSTMENTS A KEY TO JAZZ VICTORY AND TO UPCOMING GAMES.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-ADJUSTMENTS A KEY TO JAZZ VICTORY AND TO UPCOMING GAMES.

text.p: The Utah Jazz adjusted and the Chicago Bulls didn't. Result: Utah's first win of the NBA Finals. The chess game continues in Game 4 Sunday.

Both sides agreed at practice Saturday that the Jazz had made only the slightest of adjustments in Game 3 Friday night, but those small changes helped create a very big win that cut the Bulls' lead in the best-of-seven series to 2-1, with two more games in Utah.

On offence, the Jazz got Karl Malone going early -- on the way to a game-high 37 points -- by starting him away from the basket. They opened up the floor with a motion offence and ran the pick and roll better -- although Michael Jordan says his team just forgot how to defend against Utah's trademark play.
"If you spread it out it'll allow you to go more one on one and take it to the basket," said Malone.
The motion offence was the biggest surprise to the Bulls.
"That was the biggest adjustment they made, running the motion offence," said Jordan. "It kind of caught us off guard. We never really got a good feel for what they were doing.
"I don't know if they knew what they were doing, other than just moving without the ball. But I think that, looking at it on film, we'll be able to make that adjustment for Game four."
Utah point guard John Stockton said of the motion offence: "I don't think that it became our primary focus. We just wanted to get our feet moving a little bit."
The Jazz court general added: "I think the ball movement was a little bit better but more importantly, some shots fell.
"It's simple when you say it, but it's also true -- when you make a couple shots it makes it look like everybody's passing well and executing perfectly."
And why did the pick and roll work better than it had in Utah's two losses in Chicago?
"We have always said that if we can get guys in the right position on the floor we think we can execute," said Jazz coach Jerry Sloan.

Said Malone: "I think we made some minor adjustments on the pick and roll. It might not seem like that much to a lot of people but when you're two or three steps from where you're supposed to be at, that right there can make a big difference."
Jordan said the Jazz were able to exploit a Bulls' weakness in Game 3.

"We didn't execute our defensive strategy well against the pick and roll," he said. "They sensed confusion between the way we played it in Chicago and the way we played here and they attacked it. Come Sunday we have to eliminate that confusion to be on the same page and in sync defensively."
On defence, Malone said the Jazz had helped one another more. "A lot of time you get locked into trying to stop your own guy instead of helping out," he said.

The Jazz also switched their guard matchups for Game 3. Jeff Hornacek, Jordan's main defender in the first two games, guarded Scottie Pippen, and swingmen Bryon Russell and Chris Morris took the majority of shifts against Jordan.
Jordan said the Bulls hadn't taken advantage of the matchups with the smaller Hornacek enough, and Pippen agreed.

"Prior to the next game that'll be one of the focal points of our game plan to try to get me some post-ups," said Pippen, "not just for scoring opportunities but to make their defence have to react, so we can get more effective shots than shooting three-pointers and living by the jump shot."
Jordan said the Bulls -- who tied a Finals record for three-point attempts with 32 -- had taken too many long shots.
"Offensively we lived on the perimeter too much," said Jordan. "We lost our poise offensively."
Stockton felt the Jazz learned from the Bulls' defensive "clinic" in Game 2.
"They were aggressive in helping each other. I thought we gained something from that game, even though it was a beating."
But Bulls coach Phil Jackson didn't think the outcome was determined by strategic X's and O's. "I think it's all energy," he said.

Asked about intensity, Jordan, going for his fifth championship in seven years, said: "It starts today and works its way up to game time tomorrow, evaluating what you're supposed to do, evaluating what your responsibilities are, evaluating how you did last game and how you can improve that.
"That's what championship teams do."
